scenes.narration: Every time you ask an AI chatbot a question, a machine somewhere does the math. Behind the apps are the AI labs. Behind the labs are the cloud companies and the data centers. And behind almost all of them, there is one supplier.

scenes.narration: In October twenty twenty-five, that supplier, Nvidia, became the first company in history to be worth more than 5 trillion dollars.

keyframes.label: First company ever to close above it

scenes.visual_objective: Side-by-side figures count up; bars rise
scenes.narration: In its last full fiscal year, it sold 215.9 billion dollars worth of products, about eight times what it sold just three years earlier.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: For most of its life, Nvidia was known for video game graphics cards. So how did a gaming company end up at the center of the AI economy? And can it stay there? This is The Hidden Economics.

keyframes.label: Now at the center of the AI economy

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws
Axis draws; dated markers drop in on cues with ripple
scenes.narration: Nvidia was founded in 1993 in California by Jensen Huang and two fellow engineers, to make chips for computer graphics. In 1999, it launched what it calls the first GPU, a graphics processing unit. Its business was drawing video games, fast.

keyframes.label: Launches what it calls the first GPU

scenes.narration: Here is the key idea. To draw one frame of a game, a chip has to color millions of pixels, and each pixel can be worked out on its own. So instead of a few very fast workers, a graphics chip uses a huge number of simpler ones, all working at the same time.

scenes.visual_objective: CPU vs GPU: a pool of independent tasks flies into a few big cores (rounds) vs many small cores (one step); then a step-by-step chain shows the opposite trade-off
scenes.narration: Give both kinds of chip the same job: a pile of small tasks that don't depend on each other. The CPU's few powerful cores work through them in rounds. The GPU gives one to each of its many cores, and finishes in a few steps. But flip the problem. In a step-by-step job, where each step needs the result of the last one, the CPU's faster cores win. Real performance always depends on the workload.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: And training a neural network turns out to look a lot like graphics: enormous piles of multiplications that can run side by side. In 2012, a network called AlexNet, trained on two Nvidia gaming cards, won a famous image recognition contest. Researchers took notice, and so did Nvidia. In 2017, it launched its first chip with Tensor Cores, built from the ground up for AI.

keyframes.label: 2017: first Tensor Core GPU, built for AI

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws
Layered software ecosystem builds bottom-up with data pulses; optional developer counter; switching-cost panel fills item by item
scenes.narration: But the chip was only half the story. Years before AI took off, in 2006, Nvidia released CUDA, software that let programmers use its graphics chips for general computing. On top of it, Nvidia built libraries for math, for neural networks and for linking chips together. The popular AI frameworks plugged into those libraries. Developers learned them. And applications were built on top. Today Nvidia says more than 7.5 million developers use CUDA and its other tools.

scenes.visual_objective: Layered software ecosystem builds bottom-up with data pulses; optional developer counter; switching-cost panel fills item by item
scenes.narration: That creates what economists call switching costs. A company can move to another chip, but first it may have to port and retest its code, tune its performance again, change its tools, and retrain its teams. None of this is impossible. Other chips run AI every day. But every step costs time and money, and that friction is valuable to Nvidia.

scenes.visual_objective: Whiteboard hand-drawing: an original hand traces each stroke and writes labels progressively, then the sketch colours in and comes alive
scenes.narration: It is also a network effect. More developers write more software for Nvidia chips. More software attracts more customers. More customers bring in more money for new chips and new tools, which attract even more developers. The wheel feeds itself.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Now, the money. Nvidia's year ends in late January, so its fiscal twenty twenty-six is mostly calendar twenty twenty-five. For a decade, revenue grew steadily. Then it exploded: from 27 billion dollars in fiscal twenty twenty-three, to 215.9 billion dollars in fiscal twenty twenty-six.

keyframes.label: FISCAL YEARS END IN LATE JANUARY

scenes.visual_objective: Fiscal-year columns grow chronologically by business segment, then morph into a 100% share view
scenes.narration: What changed is who buys. In fiscal twenty twenty, gaming was the biggest business, and data center sales were about a quarter of the total. By fiscal twenty twenty-six, data center revenue had reached 193.7 billion dollars. That is about 90 percent of everything Nvidia sold.

Those buyers are cloud giants, AI labs and large companies building what Nvidia calls AI factories. And they are concentrated. In fiscal twenty twenty-six, one direct customer accounted for 22 percent of Nvidia's revenue, and another for 14 percent.

scenes.visual_objective: Line chart draws progressively with the narration; event annotations pop on cues
scenes.narration: Then look at the margin. Gross margin is what is left from each dollar of sales after the cost of making the product. Nvidia's rose from about 57 percent in fiscal twenty twenty-three to 75 percent in fiscal twenty twenty-five. Last year it slipped to 71 percent, partly because of a 4.5 billion dollar charge on chips it could no longer sell to China.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Why so profitable? Demand ran far ahead of supply. The product was hard to replace. And customers were not just buying chips, but whole systems: processors, networking and software that work together. Networking alone brought in 31 billion dollars last fiscal year. And Nvidia keeps reinvesting: it says it has spent more than 76 billion dollars on research and development since it was founded.

keyframes.label: A product that is hard to replace

scenes.visual_objective: Counter rolls up to the figure inside an orbiting tick ring; label and context rise in
scenes.narration: And it is still growing. In the quarter that ended in July twenty twenty-six, Nvidia brought in 96.2 billion dollars, up 106 percent from a year earlier, and it expected about 108 billion dollars in the quarter after that.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws
World map with camera moves: supply stages light up in order, packets flow along arcs, process strip tracks the stage; optional bottleneck chokes everything downstream
scenes.narration: Here is the surprising part. Nvidia designs its chips, but it does not make them. Its engineers in California send the designs to TSMC in Taiwan, which prints them onto silicon wafers. The chips are then joined with stacks of high bandwidth memory from SK Hynix, Micron and Samsung, using an advanced packaging technique called CoWoS. Contract manufacturers assemble them into servers, and the servers ship to data centers around the world.

scenes.visual_objective: World map with camera moves: supply stages light up in order, packets flow along arcs, process strip tracks the stage; optional bottleneck chokes everything downstream
scenes.narration: A chain like this is only as fast as its slowest link. Nvidia's own annual report warns that a shortage of any one component can hold back its sales. When advanced packaging or memory runs short, everything downstream has to wait.

scenes.visual_objective: Camera-driven vector map: highlighted countries, animated routes with moving packets, flow arcs with particles, pulsing markers, callouts
scenes.narration: Most of this chain is concentrated in Asia, above all in Taiwan. Nvidia is trying to spread it out. In October twenty twenty-five, it showed the first Blackwell wafer made in the United States, at TSMC's factory in Arizona. But reports say those wafers still travel back to Taiwan to be packaged.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws
Animated flow diagram: nodes pop in on cues, links draw and carry moving coins
scenes.narration: So who could challenge Nvidia? Its annual report names them: chipmakers like AMD, Intel and Huawei, and also some of its own biggest customers. Google, Amazon and Microsoft all design AI chips of their own.

scenes.visual_objective: Side-by-side figures count up; bars rise
scenes.narration: AMD sells data center GPUs too, with its own open software platform, called ROCm. In calendar twenty twenty-five, AMD's whole data center business, including its server processors, brought in 16.6 billion dollars. Nvidia's data center revenue in its latest fiscal year was 193.7 billion dollars.

scenes.visual_objective: Side-by-side figures count up; bars rise
scenes.narration: Then there are custom chips. Google builds its own TPUs, now in their seventh-generation. Amazon builds Trainium, and its Project Rainier cluster runs nearly half a million of them. In late twenty twenty-five, the AI lab Anthropic said it plans to use up to one million Google TPUs, while still using Amazon's chips and Nvidia's GPUs.

keyframes.label: up to · also uses Trainium + NVIDIA

scenes.visual_objective: Competitive matrix: a cursor selects each dimension and cells type in; then options slide onto a conceptual flexibility-vs-specialisation axis
scenes.narration: Why build your own chip? Economics. A general-purpose GPU can run almost any AI workload, has the widest software support, and can be rented from many clouds. A custom accelerator is designed around one company's own workloads. At enormous scale it can be cheaper to run, but it is mostly available inside that company's cloud, and software has to be adapted to it. Different jobs favor different chips. There is no single winner.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws
Counter rolls up to the figure inside an orbiting tick ring; label and context rise in
scenes.narration: The whole boom rests on one thing: customers spending. Trackers estimate that Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta plan to spend roughly 700 billion dollars on capital projects in twenty twenty-six, much of it on AI data centers.

scenes.visual_objective: Side-by-side figures count up; bars rise
scenes.narration: That is also the risk. If that spending slows, so does Nvidia. Its biggest customers are building rival chips. And when a customer that large pauses its orders, it shows up directly in Nvidia's revenue. Its supply chain runs through a handful of factories in Asia. And export rules have shut much of the China market: Nvidia's latest forecast assumes no data center compute sales there at all.

The market is shifting, too. A model is trained once, but it runs every time someone uses it. That second part is called inference, and as it grows, the cost of each answer matters more. That is exactly where custom chips compete. Nvidia's response is to keep moving, with new systems every year, like its next platform, Rubin, which it says will cut the cost of inference again.

keyframes.label: NVIDIA: A NEW PLATFORM EVERY YEAR (NEXT: Rubin)

scenes.visual_objective: Camera-driven vector map: highlighted countries, animated routes with moving packets, flow arcs with particles, pulsing markers, callouts
scenes.narration: Nvidia's real advantage was never one chip. It was a stack: hardware, software, developers and suppliers, built over three decades. In an economy hungry for computing power, whoever controls the bottleneck captures the profit. And one of the biggest bottlenecks of all sits on a single island. Next time: why Taiwan matters so much to the global economy. This was The Hidden Economics.
